why: The statement asks whether any K_{m,n} has a drawing with fewer than Z(m,n) crossings. The OpenAI manuscript claims cr(K_{m,n}) = Z(m,n) for all m and n, which answers that question 'no' in full, so I scored it whole. Its 'admissible drawing' class (finitely many proper crossings, no triple points) is the standard normalisation in crossing-number work, so I did not count that restriction as changing the question. Nobody qualified has checked it, so it is unreviewed: a sorry-free top-level Lean file is not digestion. I marked it doubtful rather than credible because of the release-wide errors and the history of failed proofs of this formula. The repository's statement says the model produced the results and no human author is named, so the AI role is generated. The axis drawing it exhibits is the known upper-bound construction, not what the question asks for, so object_role is null. Of the pre-snapshot events, Kleitman settles a case (min(m,n) <= 6), Woodall checks finitely many instances, and the SDP and flag-algebra papers move bounds. The 1954 and 1955 claimed proofs were knocked down by an identified gap. The Zarankiewicz-number papers, the K_{5,n}-minus-an-edge result and the rectilinear multipartite paper are variants.
doubts: The two OpenAI events describe one manuscript: one comes from the research pass, the other from the repository stage. They carry identical answers. The AI attribution is stated for the whole repository, not for this result individually. The record does not establish that the whole Lean import closure is sorry-free, nor whether the manuscript was revised after 6 Oct 2026. I scored Fabila-Monroy et al. as variant; none would serve equally well, since either way the event is discarded.
